chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man caught two birds, one from the pigeons of the Sanctuary (Haram) and the other from the pigeons of outside the Sanctuary. He said: 'He buys wheat equivalent in value to the one from the pigeons of the Sanctuary and feeds it to the pigeons of the Sanctuary, and gives in charity the compensation for the other.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And upon the one in Ihram who catches a young ostrich, the compensation is equivalent in kind from young camels. And the mention of that has already passed in detail. Then he (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And if the one in Ihram breaks an ostrich egg, he must release male camels to breed with their females in the number of what he broke; whatever is born is a sacrifice (Hady) for the House of Allah, the Exalted. If he cannot find that, then upon him is for every egg one sheep. If he cannot find that, he feeds ten poor people for every egg. If he cannot find that, he fasts for three days for every egg.
ai.seo_question: What is the compensation for breaking an ostrich egg while in Ihram?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elaborates on the jurisprudence of *Kaffarah* (expiation) for accidental transgressions during Hajj, specifically distinguishing between the sanctity of Mecca's birds and general game. It establishes a pragmatic, ability-based hierarchy of compensation—ranging from releasing breeding camels to fasting—reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on proportionality and accessibility in religious duties. The text also notes the detailed treatment of these rulings elsewhere, underscoring the systematic nature of *Fiqh* in handling minor infractions by pilgrims.
